newsitem.title: DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC OF CONGO: Fresh pressure for peace in Congo Brazzaville.
newsitem.headline: Fresh pressure for peace in Congo Brazzaville.

text.p: France and the United States joined forces on Wednesday to press for an end to a bloody month-long showdown in the Congo Republic capital Brazzaville between its president and his predecessor.

The French Foreign Ministry announced the joint approach in Paris as Brazzaville enjoyed a relative lull in fighting, two days after Gabon's mediating president Omar Bongo sent its warring parties a fresh appeal for peace.

"France and the United States have begun a joint approach to the warring parties in Congo to convince them to pursue negotiations through the international mediators' committee chaired by Omar Bongo and cease hostilities without delay," French Foreign Ministry spokesman Jacques Rummelhardt said.
He was speaking after talks in Paris on Tuesday between U.S. ambassador to Congo Aubrey Hooks and the head of the ministry's director for African affairs Jean-Didier Roisin.

Diplomats in the Democratic Republic of the Congo capital Kinshasa, across the Congo River from Brazzaville, said that the next step was likely to be meetings between national mediator Bernard Kolelas, the mayor of Brazzaville, and President Pascal Lissouba and separately with rival Denis Sassou Nguesso, but no time had been set.
Hundreds of people have been killed in the fighting that flared on June 5 when Lissouba tried to disarm Sassou's militia, ahead of presidential elections due on July 27 but now effectively postponed.
Each side says the other is responsible for sporadic firing that can be heard in Kinshasa from Brazzaville.
"It's relatively calm, but from time to time there's a last-ditch action on the part of Lissouba's forces," said Francois Iboovi, a spokesman for Sassou.
Bongo sent his latest proposals to the two protagonists on Monday, diplomats said.
Bongo, who is married to one of Sassou's daughters and is a long-standing friend of Lissouba, began his mediation three weeks ago but it has produced scant results.
Both Sassou and Lissouba say they want elections but disagree on how they can be held fairly.
The battle lines have changed little in recent days.

Sporadic firing continues in the northern districts of Talangai and Ouenze while the Bacongo quarter, which is under the control of Kolelas and his militia, remains neutral and home to thousands of residents displaced from other parts of town.
A U.N. security adviser said the area around the frontline, which runs past the city's two largest hotels, was still a no-man's land.
